section_summary: This section begins with wartime planning for a possible flight of Japan’s Emperor and senior officials, proposals to organize anti-militarist “Free Japanese,” and correspondence about American participation in such movements. It then documents Japan’s early post-surrender governmental, constitutional, party, labor, and economic changes. The largest portion consists of a detailed State Department commentary and related drafts concerning the proposed United States strategic trusteeship over the former Japanese-mandated Pacific islands.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Possible Flight of the Emperor and Japanese Officials
subfiles.about: Grew assesses the possibility that the Emperor and senior Japanese officials might flee to China or Manchuria before the occupation of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grew considers such a flight plausible but primarily a military problem that need not require fundamental changes to occupation directives. He suggests that abandonment of Japan could be treated as abdication and exploited to weaken resistance, while succession or termination of the imperial institution should await conditions after Tokyo’s occupation. Soviet entry into the war would substantially change the problem.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Note: “An International Organization of Free Japanese”
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a Chungking letter transmitting a memorandum on an international organization of Free Japanese.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies a February 9, 1945 letter from Chungking and directs researchers to file 740.0011 P.W./2-945 for the original. Its subject is the proposed creation of an international Free Japanese organization.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Emmerson’s Free Japanese Proposal
subfiles.about: The memorandum evaluates Emmerson’s proposal for an international organization of Free Japanese and recommends interdivisional review.
subfiles.summary: Johansen argues that the proposed body would inevitably acquire a political character despite being nominally unofficial. Okano’s demand for the Japanese People’s Emancipation League to participate in a future democratic government raises concerns about political entanglement and compatibility with unconditional surrender. The memorandum recommends that Emmerson prepare a paper for the Interdivisional Area Committee on the Far East and consult Blakeslee.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on an International Japanese People’s Liberation Alliance
subfiles.to: Officers of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum advocates quickly organizing overseas Japanese for psychological warfare and postwar pacification.
subfiles.summary: The writer proposes an unofficial Japanese liberation alliance whose creation could be facilitated by the Office of War Information and Office of Strategic Services. Although Okano might harbor Communist ambitions and could later figure in Soviet plans, the United States should seek to use Communist and other Japanese elements rather than rely solely on moderates. Japanese-language broadcasts and leaflets issued in the organization’s name are presented as urgent psychological-warfare tools.

subfiles.title: Request for Declassification or Downgrading of the February 14 Memorandum
subfiles.to: Office of the Assistant Secretary for Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The form requests review of the classified memorandum concerning Emmerson’s Free Japanese proposal.
subfiles.summary: The document identifies the February 14, 1945 Johansen memorandum and its subject, the despatch “An International Organization of ‘Free’ Japanese.” U. Alexis Johnson is named in the review section for the Assistant Secretary’s office.

subfiles.title: Letter Proposing an American Committee for a Free Japan
subfiles.about: Muldavin asks whether American citizens of Japanese ancestry may join a proposed American Committee for a Free Japan.
subfiles.summary: Muldavin questions how State Department policy on foreign “free movements” applies to Japanese Americans. He argues that a supervised American committee could encourage democratic elements in Japan, save American lives by appealing to soldiers and civilians, and recruit personnel for an occupation administration.
keywords: American Committee for a Free Japan

subfiles.title: Reply to Albert Muldavin on Free-Movement Policy
subfiles.about: Dickover explains U.S. policy toward American participation in foreign free movements and possible registration requirements.
subfiles.summary: Dickover states that the policy applies to all Americans regardless of racial origin and that persons born in the United States are American citizens. He notes that the Department neither encourages nor prevents private association with free movements. Muldavin is advised to consult the Department of Justice about registration under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

subfiles.title: Letter Transmitting a Study of the Japanese Board of Information
subfiles.about: Buttles transmits an unclassified study and chart on the Japanese Board of Information.
subfiles.summary: The study describes the board’s organization, composition, and probable routine using War Department information derived chiefly from monitored Japanese broadcasts. Buttles requests corrections and information from persons recently connected with the board, especially concerning coordination between warfare and propaganda.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the Japanese Board of Information Study
subfiles.about: Dickover acknowledges receipt of Buttles’s study after Eugene Dooman’s retirement.
subfiles.summary: The brief reply states that Dickover was asked to respond because Dooman had retired to private life. He thanks Buttles for making the study and chart available to the appropriate State Department officers.

subfiles.title: Post-Surrender Governmental Changes in Japan
subfiles.about: The report surveys Japanese cabinet changes, administrative reforms, new political parties, labor organization, and economic demobilization after surrender.
subfiles.summary: The report describes the Higashikuni and Shidehara cabinets, the dismantling of wartime agencies and military staffs, prospective electoral and constitutional reform, and restoration of political freedoms. It catalogues emerging Liberal, Socialist, Communist, emancipation, and peace organizations, often giving their leadership and programs. Later sections discuss industrial conversion, inflation, agriculture, labor-union organization, and political factions centered on Ugaki and Konoe.

subfiles.title: Memorandum Suggesting Revisions to SFE 142
subfiles.to: Mr. Vincent, Lt. Col. Hendrick, Capt. Sabin, Capt. Dennison, and Lt. Farley
subfiles.about: McCormack proposes changes to conclusions concerning reform of the Japanese governmental system.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum recommends requiring a constitution expressing the free will of the Japanese people, possibly through an elected constitutional convention. It also separates minimum reforms required if the monarchy is retained and renumbers the remaining paragraphs of SFE 142.

subfiles.title: Covering Memorandum on the Japanese Mandated Islands Trusteeship Commentary
subfiles.about: Green forwards a draft article-by-article commentary for use by Herschel Johnson during Security Council discussions.
subfiles.summary: The commentary concerns the proposed United States trusteeship agreement for the Japanese-mandated islands. Green states that the draft was prepared for discussion by the working team that afternoon.

subfiles.title: Second Draft Transmittal of the Article-by-Article Trusteeship Commentary
subfiles.to: Deputy Representative of the United States to the Security Council
subfiles.about: The draft instruction transmits an interpretive memorandum on every article of the proposed trusteeship agreement.
subfiles.summary: The document explains that the enclosed commentary is intended for forthcoming Security Council consideration. It notes that the most detailed discussion concerns the preamble and Articles 8 and 13, where questions are considered most likely.

subfiles.title: Commentary on the United States Draft Trusteeship Agreement for the Japanese Mandated Islands
subfiles.to: Herschel V. Johnson and the U.S. delegation to the Security Council
subfiles.about: The memorandum interprets the preamble and sixteen articles of the proposed strategic trusteeship agreement for the former Japanese-mandated Pacific islands.
subfiles.summary: The commentary explains the legal treatment of “states directly concerned,” the shift in U.S. policy toward simplified approval procedures, and the basis for treating the United States as administering authority and military occupant. It analyzes security powers, governmental and economic development, civil freedoms, trade, aviation, citizenship, international cooperation, legislation, reporting, inspection, amendment, and entry into force. Throughout, it compares the proposal with the League mandate and pending British, French, Belgian, Australian, and New Zealand trusteeship drafts while emphasizing U.S. security requirements and the welfare of the island inhabitants.

subfiles.title: Covering Memorandum for a Revised Trusteeship Statement
subfiles.to: Mr. Gross, Mr. Howard, Mr. Hiss, Mr. Blaisdell, Mr. Borton, Mr. Bancroft, Capt. Dennison, and Col. Giffen
subfiles.about: Green circulates a revised draft statement for Herschel Johnson concerning submission of the trusteeship agreement.
subfiles.summary: The new draft incorporates discussion from the previous Friday’s meeting. At Benjamin Cohen’s suggestion, Green has rewritten the introduction and conclusion so the statement can be made on behalf of the Secretary of State.

subfiles.title: Fifth Draft Statement on Submission of the Trusteeship Agreement to the Security Council
subfiles.from: Herschel V. Johnson, transmitting a message from the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The statement presents the principles and procedure underlying formal U.S. submission of the Japanese Mandated Islands trusteeship agreement.
subfiles.summary: The draft connects the proposal to American support for the League mandates system and the United Nations trusteeship system and asserts conformity with the UN Charter. It explains that Japan no longer exercises authority in the islands and that the United States does so as military occupant. It also records circulation of the draft to Security Council members, New Zealand, and the Philippines; the statement continues beyond page 71.
